newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto says will not visit war shrine.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto says will not visit war shrine.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will not visit a controversial Tokyo war shrine as long as he stays in office, he said in newspaper interviews published on Saturday.
Hashimoto's visit to the Yasukuni Shrine in July, the first such move by a Japanese prime minister since 1985, triggered bitter criticism from China, Taiwan and other Asian nations.

The visit is also at the heart of a heated border dispute between Japan on the one hand and China, Hong Kong and Taiwan on the other over small East China Sea islets called the Diaoyu in Chinese and Senkaku in Japanese.
"I have always thought the visit was a personal issue, an act that had to do with my inner feelings," Hashimoto told the joint interview with the Asahi and Yomiuri newspapers.
"But as long as I am prime minister, my actions must not invite misunderstandings or doubts against Japan."
Hashimoto was responding to a question whether he would repeat a visit to the Yasukuni Shrine, in central Tokyo.
Yasukuni enshrines the spirit of Japan's 2.6 million war dead since the late 19th century, including several Class-A war criminals such as World War Two premier General Hideki Tojo.

Before the islands dispute flared up over the construction of a makeshift lighthouse by a Japanese ultra-nationalist group, Hashimoto had said he would repeat his visit this month, during Yasukuni's autumnal festival.

Hashimoto has since officially cancelled that visit, and the Japanese government had notified the Chinese government of the cancellation. The remarks published on Saturday means he would not make further visits as long as he stayed in power.

On Friday, Japan and Taiwan tried to ease tensions over the islands dispute. Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told Taiwan representatives that Japan would not recognise the lighthouse as an official maritime aid but said it would not rescind sovereignity claims over the islands.
Separately, Taiwan negotiators said they failed to reach agreement with Japan in talks over fishing rights and other issues stemming from the sovereignty row.

Tensions have grown as Japanese coastguard cutters repelled private boats attempting to land protesters on the islands, triggering popular calls in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and China for a more forceful response from Beijing and Taipei.

Pressure on Japan to defuse tensions escalated with the September 26 death of Hong Kong activist David Chan, who drowned after jumping off a protest ship that had been prevented from putting Chan and colleagues ashore.
